Summary (auto): Deep-dive on Private/VPC security architecture, focused on ingress/egress, firewalling, KMS, audit logs, RBAC/SSO. Action items agreed.

Transcript:
[00:00] Ethan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Ethan Park from Redwood, AE on the account, and with me is Priya Nair, our SE. Quick intros?
[00:12] Lena: Hi, Lena Morales, CISO at Northstar, thanks.
[00:15] Ollie: Ollie Chen, Cloud Architect.
[00:18] Maya: Maya Patel, Security Engineer.
[00:21] Priya: Great, thanks. The goal today is to walk through our private VPC deployment model and answer detailed questions about network isolation, ingress/egress and encryption. Happy to stop and sketch diagrams.
[00:35] Lena: We're particularly focused on egress control and auditability — we can't have model traffic exfiltrating to public endpoints, and SOC2/ISO evidence is needed.
[00:44] Ethan: Absolutely; that's common. Priya will run through the architecture then we'll go deeper into KMS, audit logs and SSO.
[00:50] Priya: Ok high level: for Private we offer a VPC-hosted control plane (customer-managed VPC peering or private endpoint) and data plane that can run on customer subnets or in a managed private account. Typical patterns: private API endpoints (no public internet), NAT gateway or egress proxy for controlled outbound, VPC endpoints to S3 and KMS, and customer-managed KMS keys — we support both cloud KMS and HSM-backed keys.
[01:20] Ollie: Clarify that — so our traffic to the model weights, logs, etc., stays inside AWS using VPC endpoints? No internet traverse?
[01:28] Priya: Correct, with S3 VPC endpoints and KMS grants you can avoid public internet. We also support pushing logs to customer SIEM via private endpoints or a bastion/proxy inside the VPC.
[01:40] Lena: How do you handle model cache (KV cache) — does that write to disk in a way that could be exfiltrated? We need assurance that cached data isn't leaked to public storage.
[01:50] Priya: KV cache is ephemeral and lives on instance-local NVMe in most configs; it never leaves the VPC by default. For Dedicated/private deployments we don't push cache to public endpoints; you can configure encryption at rest using the customer KMS key.
[02:05] Maya: Encryption — do you support customer-managed keys (CMKs) and bring-your-own-HSM? We need FIPS/HSM usage for some workloads.
[02:11] Priya: Yes, we support CMKs and integration with customer HSM/KMS. For HSM we can integrate via Cloud HSM or external HSM with supported key wrapping. For FIPS outputs we can route key ops through HSM. There are a couple of implementation paths — we can walk through offline.
[02:29] [00:02:30] Ethan: Quick note — customers often want to limit egress to a small allow-list. We can lock down egress via security groups + NACLs and enforce via an egress proxy or NGFW. Priya, do we have a recommended rule template?
[02:44] Priya: Yes. Minimal egress: allow KMS endpoints, S3 VPC endpoints, and Redwood control plane private endpoint/peering IPs. Block 0.0.0.0/0 for ephemeral instances. If customers need package updates we recommend a dedicated NAT with strict allowlist or an internal update mirror. We'll share a sample firewall rule set.
[03:05] Ollie: What about DNS — we worry about DNS over HTTP exfiltration.
[03:10] Priya: Good call. We recommend internal DNS resolvers with response policy zones, plus route 53 resolver endpoints or DNS proxies that can be egress-filtered. You can also force DNS to use VPC resolver endpoints only.
[03:22] Lena: Audit logs — we need proof of all admin actions, model access, and token-level tracing. How granular are your logs? Retention options?
[03:32] Priya: We capture request metadata (requester, model, prompt size, timestamps), policy decisions (which model variant served), and system-level events (deploys, key rotations). For Private, logs can be forwarded to customer SIEM via Kinesis/Firehose or delivered to S3 VPC endpoints. Retention is configurable but by default we can keep 90 days; long-term retention to S3 Glacier can be arranged. We'll need to align with your retention policy.
[03:58] Maya: Do logs include any PII from prompts? We need guidance on redaction and masking.
[04:04] Priya: We recommend a combination of edge redaction and post-processing. Redwood can mask known PII categories before logs are stored; alternatively you can push logs to your environment and run your DLP. We'll include options in the docs.
[04:18] [00:04:30] Ethan: On RBAC/SSO — we support SAML/SSO and SCIM provisioning. You can define roles with least privilege: admin, ops, read-only, and model-deploy. Priya, talk about key access separation.
[04:31] Priya: Keys are only accessible to the runtime role; operators do not get direct plaintext key access. Customer KMS policies are used to allow the Redwood runtime to decrypt model artifacts or cache with limited scope. For audit we log KMS decrypt operations.
[04:48] Ollie: How do you prevent privileged users at Redwood from accessing customer data?
[04:53] Priya: For Private deployments the control plane can be customer-managed; for managed control plane we offer strict role separation, bastion access controls, and we can provide audit trails of any support access. We also support just-in-time support access with session recording.
[05:08] Lena: Support access — do you require a separate approval flow? We need an approval ticket in our system before any session.
[05:13] Ethan: Yes, we can implement an approval workflow and record sessions. We'll add that to the SOW.
[05:18] Maya: Network microsegmentation — can we put model runtime nodes in private subnets with no route to internet and only allow egress through inspected egress proxies?
[05:26] Priya: Absolutely. Typical architecture: private subnets with no IGW, NATless design; egress via an internal proxy/NGFW in a separate subnet. Alternatively, use a managed egress VPC endpoint with allow-listed endpoints.
[05:39] Ollie: What about firewalling between tenants? If we run multi-tenant on dedicated infra, how do you isolate tenants?
[05:45] Priya: We recommend either per-tenant subnets with security groups and IAM isolation or per-tenant clusters. For Dedicated we can carve GPU pools per-tenant; for Private deployments you can fully isolate at network layer. We maintain tenant scoping at the runtime and control plane levels.
[06:00] [00:06:30] Lena: Compliance artifacts: we'll need SOC2 Type II report, ISO27001 cert, penetration test summaries, and data processing addendum.
[06:10] Ethan: We'll send SOC2/ISO certificates and our penetration testing summary. We'll also include our subprocessors list and DPA.
[06:18] Maya: Regarding model artifact storage: where are model weights stored and how are they encrypted?
[06:24] Priya: We can store weights in customer S3 buckets (preferred) with SSE-KMS using your CMK, or in the managed S3 bucket with KMS keys that we grant you access to audit. In either case, weights are encrypted at rest and access is limited via IAM policies and per-blob grants.
[06:42] Ollie: For air-gapped/on-prem — what's required?
[06:46] Priya: For fully air-gapped we provide an on-prem bundle that includes the runtime container images and configuration scripts. You manage network and KMS locally; we provide installation runbook. For hybrid VPC, the control plane can be private and we use private peering.
[06:59] Lena: Patching and CVE management — how often do you push updates to runtime? We need SLA on patching windows.
[07:06] Priya: We have regular monthly patch windows and urgent CVE patches pushed as needed. For Private/on-prem customers, patching can be scheduled with you — we can provide the patch artifacts and a validation plan.
[07:18] [00:07:45] Maya: Logging format — is it JSON structured logs with consistent fields? We want to ingest to Splunk.
[07:25] Priya: Yes, structured JSON logs with fields for timestamp, request_id, user_id, operation, model, and anonymized prompt hash. We will share the schema.
[07:35] Ollie: Are there options to scrub prompt contents entirely from logs?
[07:39] Priya: Yes — you can disable request bodies from being logged or configure client-side redaction before sending. For compliance-sensitive flows we recommend client-side redaction and storing only metadata.
[07:51] Ethan: On network controls, we also support VPC peering and AWS PrivateLink endpoints for minimal blast radius. PrivateLink is nice because you can enforce endpoint policies.
[07:59] Ollie: What about egress to external model registries (if we want to pull third-party weights)?
[08:04] Priya: That would need explicit allowlisting. Ideally you'd mirror artifacts into an internal registry or S3 bucket via secure pipeline, then use internal endpoints.
[08:15] Lena: Auditability for key rotations — we need to show key versions used to encrypt specific model blobs.
[08:21] Priya: We record KMS key IDs and key version metadata alongside object metadata. We can provide logs of decrypt operations tied to request IDs.
[08:31] [00:08:45] Maya: For SIEM ingestion, do you push logs as they happen or batch?
[08:36] Priya: We provide both streaming (Kinesis/Firehose) and batch (S3) delivery. Streaming is recommended for real-time alerting.
[08:44] Ollie: Any recommendations for IDS/IPS?
[08:47] Priya: Use a managed NGFW with application-layer inspection on the egress proxy. Combine with flow logs + Suricata/IDS if you want deeper packet inspection. We have guidance for tuning to avoid false positives with high throughput model traffic.
[09:00] Ethan: Time to surface a couple of edge cases: 1) model hallucination exfil — not exactly infrastructure but we should consider prompt/data leakage in outputs; 2) debugging support sessions where we may need access to traces.
[09:12] Lena: On debugging sessions we need playbooks that minimize data exposure. Session recordings should be redacted.
[09:17] Priya: We can provide configurable session redaction and access justifications.
[09:21] [00:09:30] Maya: Do you provide a separate audit trail for support engineer console actions? We need immutable logs.
[09:27] Priya: Yes — support access is recorded with session start/end, commands executed and a transcript. These logs are immutable and can be forwarded to your S3.
[09:36] Ollie: Performance tradeoffs — does strict egress filtering add significant latency?
[09:40] Priya: Minimal. Egress proxies introduce small overhead but are typically sub-100ms per-request added latency; the bigger impact is if you have synchronous calls to external registries. Model runtime paths are local in VPC so latency is minimal.
[09:55] Ethan: We've hit a lot of items. Quick recap and next steps?
[09:59] Lena: Yes please.
[10:01] Ethan: Recap: Redwood to send SOC2/ISO artifacts and pen test summary; Priya to produce VPC ingress/egress diagram and firewall templates; customer to share egress allowlist and log retention requirements; schedule a pilot week to validate egress and KV cache. Anything to add?
[10:18] Ollie: Please include example IAM policy snippets for S3/KMS access.
[10:21] Priya: Will do.
[10:23] Maya: Also include the support access approval flow in the SOW.
[10:26] Ethan: Great, we'll follow up with docs. Thanks everyone.
[10:30] Lena: Thanks, bye.
